Transcript: Picture eastern Washington State. Across a huge area, the soil's been stripped down to bare black basalt, and the rock is cut by dry channels, some with cliffs taller than a ten-story building. There are dry waterfalls, empty plunge pools, gravel bars the size of hills. Geologists call it the Channeled Scablands.

In the 1920s a geologist named J Harlen Bretz argued that all of this was carved quickly, by an enormous flood. Now, you have to understand how that sounded at the time. Geology had been built on the idea that slow, ordinary processes, working over immense spans of time, explain the landscape. A sudden catastrophe sounded like a return to Noah's flood, like religion sneaking back into science. So when Bretz presented his case to a meeting of geologists in 1927, he got a very cold reception.

But here's the part that gets left out when this is told as a lone genius against closed minds. His critics asked a fair question: where did the water come from? A flood that size needs a source, and Bretz, at first, couldn't name one. Without it, his theory really was incomplete.

The answer came from another geologist, Joseph Pardee, who'd been studying an ancient lake in western Montana, Lake Missoula. It formed when a tongue of the ice sheet blocked a river valley and water piled up behind it. When that ice dam gave way, the lake emptied in a rush. Pardee later described giant ripple marks on the old lake floor, ripples several meters high.

So Bretz was right, and spectacularly so, except on one point. His early papers described essentially one great flood. Later work found stacked flood layers suggesting dozens, as the ice dam formed and failed again and again. The catastrophe happened, but it happened repeatedly.

Transcript: Many of you know the marshmallow test. Around 1970, Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford sat preschoolers down with a treat, a marshmallow, say, and offered a deal: eat this one now, or wait until I come back and get two. Then the adult left the room. Some kids ate the treat within seconds. Others held out the whole time by covering their eyes, singing, turning away.

What made the test famous came years later. When the researchers followed up, the children who'd waited longer tended, on average, to do better as teenagers, including higher test scores. And the popular conclusion was that the test measured willpower, a fixed trait you either had at four or didn't.

In 2013, a team at the University of Rochester asked a question that's easy to overlook. Why should a child believe the adult will come back? Before the test, an adult made the children a promise, better art supplies, for instance. For half of them, the adult kept the promise. For the other half, the adult came back empty-handed. Then came the marshmallow. The children who'd been let down waited, on average, about three minutes. The others waited roughly four times as long.

So for some children, eating the marshmallow right away may not be a failure of self-control at all. If the adults in your life don't reliably keep their word, grabbing the sure thing is a sensible bet.

Now, I want to be careful here. The Rochester study doesn't show that self-control is imaginary, or that it doesn't matter. Mischel's patterns are still worth taking seriously. What the new study shows is that the test, on its own, can't tell the two things apart. A child who eats the treat might lack patience, or might simply have learned not to trust promises.

Transcript: For most of the twentieth century, the policy on American public lands was simple: put out every wildfire, as fast as possible. For years, the official goal was to have any new fire under control by ten the next morning. And for decades, it seemed to work. The area burned each year dropped.

Then ecologists looked closely at the dry ponderosa pine forests of the American Southwest. Scars left inside old trees showed these forests had once burned often, every few years to every couple of decades, but gently. Low fires crept along the ground, burning grass and seedlings and leaving the big, thick-barked pines standing. Take those fires away, and the seedlings survive. The forest fills in with small trees, dead wood piles up, and when a fire finally does come, it climbs the small trees into the canopy and kills everything. In those forests, suppression didn't prevent fire. It postponed it and made it worse.

That argument's well supported, and it changed policy. But here's where it got stretched. In 1988, fires burned across roughly a third of Yellowstone National Park, and plenty of commentators blamed a century of suppression. A number of fire ecologists objected. Yellowstone is mostly lodgepole pine, high up, cold and fairly moist. Those forests, as far as the evidence shows, never had frequent gentle fires. They typically go well over a century without much burning, and then a hot, dry, windy summer brings huge fires that kill whole stands. That's their normal pattern. So suppression probably changed rather little there, because there wasn't much fire to suppress in the first place.

So what's the lesson? Not that putting out fires is always a mistake. It's that the right fire policy depends on what kind of fire a particular forest has lived with.

For years, the official goal was to have any new fire under control by ten the next morning. And for decades, it seemed to work. The area burned each year dropped.

Then ecologists looked closely at the dry ponderosa pine forests of the American Southwest. Scars left inside old trees showed these forests had once burned often, every few years to every couple of decades, but gently. Low fires crept along the ground, burning grass and seedlings and leaving the big, thick-barked pines standing. Take those fires away, and the seedlings survive. The forest fills in with small trees, dead wood piles up, and when a fire finally does come, it climbs the small trees into the canopy and kills everything. In those forests, suppression didn't prevent fire. It postponed it and made it worse.

That argument's well supported, and it changed policy. But here's where it got stretched. In 1988, fires burned across roughly a third of Yellowstone National Park, and plenty of commentators blamed a century of suppression. A number of fire ecologists objected. Yellowstone is mostly lodgepole pine, high up, cold and fairly moist. Those forests, as far as the evidence shows, never had frequent gentle fires. They typically go well over a century without much burning, and then a hot, dry, windy summer brings huge fires that kill whole stands. That's their normal pattern. So suppression probably changed rather little there, because there wasn't much fire to suppress in the first place.

So what's the lesson? Not that putting out fires is always a mistake. It's that the right fire policy depends on what kind of fire a particular forest has lived with.

Transcript: When you picture ancient Greek sculpture, you probably see white marble: gleaming, pure, serious. That image owes a lot to the eighteenth century, and especially to the German scholar Johann Winckelmann, who praised the white surfaces of ancient statues as the height of beauty. Generations of artists and museums followed his lead.

The trouble is, the statues weren't meant to be white. Ancient writers mention painted sculpture, and researchers have found traces of pigment on many pieces. Sometimes you can see them with the naked eye. More often you need ultraviolet light, or light shone at a low angle across the surface, which shows where paint once protected the stone from weathering. Some color survives in folds and crevices. So the case that Greek sculpture was painted is about as solid as anything in classical archaeology.

Now, in recent decades, researchers have made full-size painted copies of famous statues, and these have toured museums around the world. And a lot of visitors find them, well, shocking. Bright, flat blocks of color, a bit like a toy. Some critics have said the Greeks would never have produced anything so crude.

You might think that's just Winckelmann's taste talking again. Partly, maybe. But the critics have a point. What usually survives is the first layer, the base color. Shading, blending, fine finishing: those would've been the thinnest layers on top, and they're exactly the ones least likely to last. So a reconstruction built from surviving traces may get the colors right and still get the overall look wrong. Some of the reconstructors say as much themselves. They describe their copies as hypotheses to be tested, not final answers.

So yes, let's drop the white statues. But let's be careful not to swap one confident image for another.

Transcript: Why is ice slippery? It sounds like it has an obvious answer, and for a long time textbooks gave one. Here's the version you may have learned. When a skater stands on ice, all her weight presses down on a thin blade. That pressure lowers the melting point of the ice, so a film of water forms under the blade, and she glides on the water.

Now, there's real physics in that. Ice is unusual. Unlike most solids, it's less dense than its liquid, which is why it floats, and that's also why squeezing it can lower its melting point. So far, so good.

The problem is the numbers. When physicists worked them out, the effect turned out to be small: a few degrees at most, by most estimates, even under a narrow blade. Yet people skate perfectly well at fifteen or twenty degrees below zero. And pressure can't explain why an ordinary shoe, with a broad sole spreading your weight out, slips on ice too. So pressure melting can't be the main story.

What replaced it? Two ideas, and they're partners more than rivals. One is friction. A moving blade rubs the surface, and the heat from that rubbing can melt a very thin layer. That fits skating nicely. But friction needs motion, and ice is slippery the instant you step onto it.

The other idea goes back to Michael Faraday in the 1850s. He suggested that the surface of ice carries a thin, liquid-like layer, even well below freezing, because the molecules at the surface have fewer neighbors holding them in place. Modern experiments have broadly backed him up, though exactly how that layer behaves is still argued about.

So here's where we are. We understand why the old explanation fails better than we understand the full new one.

item.correct_answer: Why ice is slippery is less settled than often assumed

Transcript: Ask people what happened to the Library of Alexandria and you'll usually hear about one great fire, a single terrible day when the learning of the ancient world went up in smoke. Who lit it depends on who's telling the story. Julius Caesar is the favorite suspect. Others blame Christian mobs in the late fourth century, or the Arab conquest in the seventh.

Let's take these in turn. The Arab story is the weakest. The earliest versions we have were written something like six centuries after the conquest, and most historians now treat them as unreliable. The Christian episode is real: in 391 a temple called the Serapeum was destroyed. But it's not clear how many books, if any, were still kept there by then.

Caesar's more interesting. During his war in Alexandria in 48 BCE, fire spread from the harbor, and ancient writers say books burned. But some of those may have been scrolls stored in warehouses near the docks, not the library's own collection. And scholars kept working in Alexandria for generations afterward.

So if there was no single fire, what happened? Think about what a library of papyrus scrolls needed. Papyrus wears out, especially when it's handled a lot, so scrolls had to be copied again and again by trained staff, and staff have to be paid. The library ran on royal money and royal interest. In 145 BCE, King Ptolemy the Eighth drove many scholars out of the city. Later rulers had other priorities, and the city itself was fought over repeatedly.

Now, I'm not saying the fires didn't matter. They probably destroyed real things. But a collection like that doesn't need to be burned to vanish. Stop paying the copyists, wait a few generations, and it disappears anyway.

Transcript: Every seventeen years, in parts of the eastern United States, the ground opens up. Billions of periodical cicadas crawl out at once, climb the trees, sing for a few weeks, mate, lay their eggs, and die. The young drop to the soil, burrow down, and feed on root sap in the dark until, seventeen years later, they all come up together again. Some broods, mostly farther south, run on a thirteen-year cycle instead.

Two questions, then. Why come out all at once? And why those particular numbers?

The first has a well-supported answer: predator satiation. A cicada is easy prey. It's slow, loud, and defenseless. But when cicadas come up by the million, birds and squirrels eat until they can't eat any more, and most of the cicadas survive. Field studies have found that survival tends to be higher where emergences are denser. So there's a real advantage to being part of the crowd, and a real cost to coming up a year early, alone.

Now, the second question. You'll often hear that thirteen and seventeen are prime numbers, and that this is the whole point. Suppose a predator's population peaked every five years. It would line up with a seventeen-year cicada only once every eighty-five years. A prime cycle, the argument goes, keeps cicadas from matching any enemy that booms on a shorter cycle.

It's a lovely argument. The trouble is, nobody has found the predators. There's no known enemy that tracks cicadas on a fixed multi-year cycle. So the story is built around a villain who may not exist. Some researchers propose other reasons, for instance that prime cycles reduce how often different broods come up in the same year, which might keep their timing from blurring.

So here's where I land. The crowding is explained. The primes are still an open question, however satisfying the arithmetic.

Transcript: In 1905 the German sociologist Max Weber published one of the most famous arguments in the field, usually called the Protestant ethic thesis. Weber noticed that in the Germany of his day, Protestants tended to be better off than Catholics, more often business owners and skilled workers. His explanation was cultural. Certain Protestant teachings, he argued, led people to treat hard work and careful saving as a religious duty, while spending on luxury was frowned upon. Work a lot, consume little, and you build up capital. So a religious outlook, without anyone intending it, helped produce the spirit of modern capitalism.

It's an elegant idea, and people have argued about it ever since. Historians pointed to booming commerce in Catholic cities like Venice and Florence long before the Reformation. But the most interesting challenge came more recently, from two economists who went back to Prussian census data from the 1870s. That census recorded religion, and, crucially, whether people could read.

Here's what they noticed. Martin Luther wanted every believer to read the Bible for themselves, and Protestant regions pushed hard for schooling. So Protestants weren't just Protestant. On average, they were also much more literate. And when the researchers took literacy into account, most of the economic gap between Protestant and Catholic counties disappeared.

Now, notice what that does and doesn't overturn. Weber was right that Protestantism went along with prosperity. The religion still mattered. What's in doubt is his mechanism. The advantage may have come less from an attitude toward work than from a practical skill, reading, that the religion happened to promote.

So whose side am I on? The data favor the literacy explanation, though they can't rule out that a work ethic added something. And the general lesson is worth keeping: a pattern can be real while the story attached to it is wrong.

Transcript: There's an old advertising line: a diamond is forever. Chemically speaking, that's a strange thing to say, because diamond isn't the most stable form of carbon at the Earth's surface. Graphite is, the soft gray stuff in your pencil. At ordinary temperature and pressure, if you compare the energy of the two, graphite comes out slightly lower, and systems tend to move toward lower energy. So by that reasoning, every diamond ought to be turning into graphite. Right now. On your finger.

So why isn't anyone's engagement ring going gray? Here we need to separate two questions that the word 'stable' tends to blur together. Thermodynamics tells you which direction a change would go, if it happened. It tells you nothing about how fast. For speed you need kinetics, and the key idea there is an energy barrier. To rearrange diamond into graphite, you'd have to break carbon bonds that are extremely strong, and at room temperature almost no atoms ever have enough energy to get over that hump. So the change is allowed, but it's far too slow to notice in any human lifetime, and by some estimates it would take longer than the age of the universe.

You already know examples of this. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can sit quietly in a container, even though turning into water would release a lot of energy. Give it a spark, which lifts some molecules over the barrier, and it goes off violently.

Now, I don't want you to conclude that diamond is indestructible. Heat it strongly without air, and its surface does start turning into graphite. Heat it in air, and it burns. Forever, in other words, has conditions attached.

So whenever someone calls a substance stable, ask two things: stable compared with what, and stable over how long?

Transcript: For a long time painters had a convention for a galloping horse. Look at a famous racing picture from the early nineteenth century, Géricault's Derby at Epsom, and you'll see the horses stretched out like rocking horses, front legs reaching forward, back legs reaching back, all four in the air. It looked fast. Nobody could check it, because a horse's legs move too quickly for the eye to follow.

In the 1870s the railroad tycoon Leland Stanford, a former governor of California, hired the photographer Eadweard Muybridge to settle whether a running horse ever has all four feet off the ground at once. You'll often hear that Stanford had a huge bet riding on it. There's little solid evidence for that, so I'd treat it as legend. What's well documented is the method. In 1878 Muybridge lined up a row of cameras along a track, with shutters fast enough to freeze the legs, firing in sequence as the horse went by.

And the answer was yes, all four feet do leave the ground. But not the way painters showed it. The moment in the air comes when the legs are gathered underneath the body, not when they're stretched out. The rocking-horse pose never happens.

You'd think that would end it: science wins, painters lose. But the sculptor Auguste Rodin raised a sharp objection. He argued that it's the photograph that lies, because real time never stops. A frozen instant shows a position the eye never actually sees, so it can look stiff and stalled. A painting that blends several moments may convey the experience of speed more truthfully.

I think Rodin had a point, though a narrower one than he claimed. As a record of where the legs are, the photograph wins outright. As a record of what a gallop looks like to someone watching, it isn't obviously better.

Transcript: Your weather app says thirty percent chance of rain tomorrow. What does that actually mean? When researchers asked people in several cities, in Europe and in New York, they got a startling range of answers. Some said it'll rain thirty percent of the time. Some said it'll rain over thirty percent of the area. Others said that thirty percent of forecasters think it'll rain.

The official definition, at least for the US National Weather Service, is this: it's the chance that measurable rain, at least a hundredth of an inch, falls at any given point in the forecast area during the forecast period. So, roughly: stand in one spot, and there's a thirty percent chance you'll get wet. Notice what it doesn't say. It says nothing about how long it'll rain, or how hard.

So it sounds as if the public is just confused. And partly that's true. But I want to suggest the confusion isn't entirely the public's fault.

Here's why. Forecasters often treat the number as two things multiplied together: how confident they are that rain will develop somewhere in the area, and how much of the area they expect it to cover. Now run that both ways. A forecaster who's certain that showers will hit about thirty percent of the region gives you thirty percent. A forecaster who thinks there's a thirty percent chance that a storm will arrive and soak everybody also gives you thirty percent. Those are very different days. On one, scattered showers, and you may well stay dry. On the other, it's all or nothing.

So the people who said 'thirty percent of the area' weren't inventing something from nowhere. They'd caught half of the way the number gets made. The single figure hides which situation you're in, and if you're planning an outdoor wedding, that's exactly what you'd want to know.

Transcript: Unglazed clay pots are porous, and when you cook or store food in them, fats soak into the walls. Some survive for thousands of years. Grind up a scrap of pottery, extract the residue, and chemistry can often tell you whether the fat came from plants, from meat, or from milk. Milk fat has a distinctive chemical signature, and this kind of analysis has pushed evidence for dairying back a long way, to some of the earliest farming communities in western Asia and southeastern Europe, roughly eight or nine thousand years ago.

So the obvious picture is: these people kept cattle, sheep, or goats, and they drank the milk. But there's a problem, and it comes from genetics. Most adult humans, then and now, lose much of their ability to digest lactose, the main sugar in milk, after childhood. The genetic variants that let adults go on digesting it are common in some populations today. Yet ancient DNA suggests they were rare among early farmers, and spread widely only thousands of years after the first milk residues.

So early farmers had a food that would give most adults stomach trouble. What did they do? One answer comes from pottery again. In Poland, archaeologists studied clay vessels pierced with small holes, about seven thousand years old, and found milk fats in them. They look very much like cheese strainers. Making cheese, or yogurt for that matter, removes or breaks down much of the lactose. So processing may be how people got milk's benefits without the discomfort.

Here's the broader point, though. A residue tells you that milk was in the pot. It doesn't tell you who ate it, how it was prepared, or how much. That has to come from other evidence: the shape of the vessel, the genes, the animal bones. Chemistry gives you the ingredient, not the recipe.

Transcript: Unglazed clay pots are porous, and when you cook or store food in them, fats soak into the walls. Some survive for thousands of years. Grind up a scrap of pottery, extract the residue, and chemistry can often tell you whether the fat came from plants, from meat, or from milk. Milk fat has a distinctive chemical signature, and this kind of analysis has pushed evidence for dairying back a long way, to some of the earliest farming communities in western Asia and southeastern Europe, roughly eight or nine thousand years ago.

So the obvious picture is: these people kept cattle, sheep, or goats, and they drank the milk. But there's a problem, and it comes from genetics. Most adult humans, then and now, lose much of their ability to digest lactose, the main sugar in milk, after childhood. The genetic variants that let adults go on digesting it are common in some populations today. Yet ancient DNA suggests they were rare among early farmers, and spread widely only thousands of years after the first milk residues.

So early farmers had a food that would give most adults stomach trouble. What did they do? One answer comes from pottery again. In Poland, archaeologists studied clay vessels pierced with small holes, about seven thousand years old, and found milk fats in them. They look very much like cheese strainers. Making cheese, or yogurt for that matter, removes or breaks down much of the lactose. So processing may be how people got milk's benefits without the discomfort.

Here's the broader point, though. A residue tells you that milk was in the pot. It doesn't tell you who ate it, how it was prepared, or how much. That has to come from other evidence: the shape of the vessel, the genes, the animal bones. Chemistry gives you the ingredient, not the recipe.
